lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding free job help near you
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Find your nearest American Job Center and one other free place to get job help.
This lesson builds toward: Using CareerOneStop or the 1-877-US-2JOBS line, you will find your nearest American Job Center and one other free place to get job help, writing down its address, phone and hours.
American Job Centers are public job centers across the country. They help job seekers with job searches, referrals and placement, and many also offer computers, workshops and training information. Some services have rules about who qualifies and can vary by state.
You can find your nearest center with the American Job Center Finder on CareerOneStop, a U.S. Department of Labor website, or by calling 1-877-US-2JOBS.
Public libraries also help with job searches, résumé printing and free computer time. Real job help never asks you to pay to get a job.
Step by step:
- Open the American Job Center Finder on careeronestop.org, or call 1-877-US-2JOBS.
- Type your ZIP code or city.
- Write down the nearest center's address, phone and hours.
- Ask your library what job-search help it offers.
Words to know:
- American Job Center: a public center that helps people find work and training.
- Referral: when a center sends you to a job or a program that may fit you.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Labor: American Job Centers
- CareerOneStop: American Job Center Finder
Try it now: Find the American Job Center nearest you and write down its address, phone number and hours.
You can now find free, official job help near you.

options: A U.S. Department of Labor website that helps you find job centers
check.why: CareerOneStop is a Department of Labor site with the American Job Center Finder.

check.q: You need to print résumés and use a computer for free. Where else can you go?
options: A website that charges a sign-up fee
check.why: Public libraries help with job searches, printing and free computer time.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Naming your skills, paid and unpaid
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your work and life experience into a list of job skills.
This lesson builds toward: Given your paid and unpaid experience, you will list the job skills it shows with an AI assistant, keeping only skills you can give a real example of.
Many people say "I don't have skills" when they really do. Caring for children or an older parent, running a household budget, cooking for a church event, fixing cars for neighbors or doing cash jobs all build real skills.
Tell an AI assistant what you have done, in plain words, and ask it to turn that into job skills. For example: "For five years I cared for my grandmother, managed her medicines and appointments, and kept the household budget. What job skills does this show?"
Pick the skills that are true and that you can give an example of. Do not keep anything you cannot back up in an interview.
Step by step:
- Write down everything you have done: paid jobs, cash jobs, caregiving, volunteering, school.
- Ask the AI to list the job skills each one shows.
- Keep only skills you can give a real example of.
- Save the list for your résumé.
Words to know:
- Skill: something you know how to do well, like scheduling, customer service or using a cash register.
- Transferable skill: a skill from one part of life that helps in a different job.
Try it now: Write down three things you have done (paid or unpaid). Ask an AI assistant to name the job skills each one shows. Keep the ones you can give a real example for.
You can now turn your paid and unpaid experience into an honest list of job skills.

check.q: Which is an unpaid experience that builds job skills?
check.why: Cooking for an event shows planning, teamwork and food handling skills.

check.q: The AI says your babysitting shows "project management" but you cannot give an example. What do you do?
check.why: Only keep skills you can back up with a real example in an interview.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing a one-page résumé with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a simple one-page résumé with an AI assistant and a free document tool.
This lesson builds toward: Given your skills list and history, you will write a one-page résumé with an AI assistant and a free document tool, with every main part and no Social Security number or birth date.
A résumé is a one-page summary of your skills and experience. A simple, clean résumé is better than a fancy one.
Give the AI your skills list, your jobs or activities with dates, and any training or school. Ask for a one-page résumé with these parts: contact line, short summary, skills, experience, and education or training.
Do not put your Social Security number, birth date or full ID numbers on a résumé or in the AI. Type your phone and email into the final document yourself. Copy the result into a free tool like Google Docs or Microsoft Word on the web, and save it as a PDF to send.
Step by step:
- Give the AI your skills, jobs or activities with dates, and training.
- Ask for a one-page résumé: contact line, summary, skills, experience, education.
- Copy it into Google Docs or Word on the web.
- Add your phone and email yourself; leave out Social Security number and birth date.
- Read it out loud, fix mistakes, and save it as a PDF.
Words to know:
- Résumé: a one-page summary of your skills, work and training for employers.
- PDF: a file type that keeps your document looking the same on any device.
Try it now: Use your skills list from Lesson 2 to ask an AI assistant for a one-page résumé. Copy it into Google Docs or Word on the web and read it out loud.
You can now write a simple one-page résumé with AI and a free document tool.

check.q: Which parts belong on a simple résumé?
options: Contact line, summary, skills, experience, education or training
Social Security number and birth date
check.why: These five parts give employers what they need on one page.

check.q: When should you add your phone and email to the résumé?
options: Type them into the AI first
Type them into the final document yourself
check.why: Adding them yourself in the document keeps private details out of the AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Matching your résumé to a job posting
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Change your résumé so it matches what a real job posting asks for.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real job posting, you will change your résumé to match the posting's skills and words, using only true information and saving a copy named for that job.
Employers want to see that you fit their job. A job posting lists what they need. When your résumé uses the same skills and words, it is easier to see the match.
Paste the job posting and your résumé into the AI and ask: "Which skills in this posting do I already show? Suggest changes to my résumé so it matches better, using only true information."
Keep it honest. Matching means showing your real skills in the employer's words, not adding things you have not done.
Step by step:
- Find a real job posting you could apply for.
- Paste the posting and your résumé into the AI (no private numbers).
- Ask which skills match and what to change, using only true information.
- Update your résumé and save a new copy named for that job.
Words to know:
- Job posting: a notice from an employer describing a job and what they need.
- Keywords: important words from the job posting, like "customer service" or "forklift".
Try it now: Find one real job posting near you. Ask an AI assistant to compare it to your résumé and suggest honest changes. Save a new copy for that job.
You can now match your résumé to a real job posting honestly.

options: Using the same font as the employer
Showing your real skills in the employer's words
check.why: Matching shows your true skills using the words the posting uses.

check.q: The posting asks for "customer service" and you helped shoppers at a cash job. What do you do?
options: Describe it as customer service, with the true details
check.why: Your real experience fits their keyword, so you say it honestly in their words.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Practicing for the interview
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Practice answering common interview questions with an AI assistant.
This lesson builds toward: With an AI assistant acting as the interviewer, you will answer common interview questions out loud with short real stories, asking for and using one tip on each answer.
Interviews feel easier with practice. An AI assistant can play the interviewer. Ask: "Act as an interviewer for this job. Ask me one common question at a time and wait for my answer. After each answer, give me one tip."
Common questions include: "Tell me about yourself." "Why do you want this job?" "Tell me about a time you solved a problem." Use a short real story: what happened, what you did, and how it turned out.
Say your answers out loud, not just in your head. If you have a gap in work history, practice one honest, short sentence about it and then talk about what you are ready to do now.
Step by step:
- Ask the AI to act as the interviewer for your job posting.
- Answer one question at a time, out loud, then type it in.
- Use a short real story: what happened, what you did, the result.
- Ask for one tip after each answer and try again.
Words to know:
- Interview: a meeting where an employer asks you questions to decide whether to hire you.
- Work gap: a time when you were not in a paid job.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to interview you for the job from Lesson 4. Answer two questions out loud, type your answers, and ask for one tip each.
You can now practice interview answers with AI and improve them with feedback.

check.q: What should you ask the AI to do after each practice answer?
options: Give one tip to improve it
check.why: One tip at a time helps you make each answer better.

check.q: The interviewer asks about a two-year gap when you cared for family. What do you say?
options: One honest, short sentence, then what you are ready to do now
Talk about it for ten minutes
check.why: A short honest answer, then a focus on what you can do now, is strongest.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Spotting job scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Recognize the warning signs of a job scam and know what to do.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job offer or posting, you will check it for the warning signs of a job scam and confirm the company yourself, before you share any bank or Social Security number.
Job scams target people who need work. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) warns that honest employers will never ask you to pay to get a job.
Other warning signs: they send you a check and ask you to send part of the money back or buy gift cards; they promise big pay for little work; the job is receiving and reshipping packages; or the offer comes out of nowhere.
If an offer looks too good, stop. Look up the company yourself, call its real phone number, or ask at your American Job Center. Never give your bank or Social Security number before you have confirmed a real job.
Step by step:
- Never pay to get a job.
- Never deposit a check and send money back.
- Look up the company yourself and call its real number.
- Ask your American Job Center if you are unsure.
Words to know:
- Fake check scam: a scammer sends a check, asks you to send part back, then the check bounces and you owe the bank.
- FTC: the Federal Trade Commission, the U.S. agency that protects consumers from scams.
Official sources:
- FTC: Job Scams
Try it now: Final task: with your résumé matched to a real posting, have the AI ask you three interview questions, answer each out loud, and ask for one tip to improve each answer. Check the posting for any scam warning signs.
You can now apply for a real job with a matched résumé, practice the interview, and spot job scams.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds One-page résumé Longer than a page, parts missing, or private numbers included. One page with contact line, summary, skills, experience and education, and no private numbers. Read out loud, mistakes fixed, and saved as a PDF. Matched to the posting The résumé does not use the posting's skills or words, or adds untrue things. Uses the posting's key skills in true statements. Saved as a separate copy named for that job. Real skills Lists skills the learner cannot give an example of. Every skill has a real example from paid or unpaid work. Includes unpaid skills like caregiving or volunteering with clear examples. Interview answers Fewer than three answers, or not said out loud. Three questions answered out loud, with one tip asked for on each. Tried each answer again using the tip, with a short real story. Scam check Did not check the posting for warning signs. Checked the posting for scam signs and looked up the company. Can name which warning signs were and were not present. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a warning sign of a job scam?
options: A posting with a real company address
An interview at the company office
Big pay promised for very little work
A job listed at your American Job Center
check.why: Offers that promise big pay for little work are a common scam sign.

check.q: A new "employer" texts asking for your bank number before any interview. What do you do?
options: Send it so you get paid faster
Ask a friend to send theirs
Stop and look up the company yourself
check.why: Never give your bank number before you have confirmed a real job.
